newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: TWO DEAD AND 50 HOMES LOST IN VICTORIAN FIRES
Two people are dead and 50 homes destroyed, in the Dandenong Ranges, east of Melbourne, after yesterday's bushfires.
The cost of the yesterday's fires, which burned in a number of areas across Victoria, is still being added up, but insurance experts are already estimating it's into millions of dollars.
At Ferny Creek, in the heart of the Dandenongs, a 26-year-old man and a 25-year-old woman died in a house, and arson squad detectives are at the house this morning, sifting through the remains.
All around the area, three hundred Country Fire Authority volunteers and 150 of their metropolitian counterparts are still watching trouble spots.
WRITERS SIGN DECLARATION AGAINST LIBRARY CHANGES
Twenty-five of Australia's leading writers have signed a declaration claiming government cuts are eroding their rights.
The writers, including Dorothy Hewett, Donald Horne and Ruth Park, are upset at a proposal for a 25 year limit on payments to authors whose works appear in public libraries.
The authors claim their livelihood is being threatened.
The cuts to the Public Lending Right Scheme are expected to save the government about half-a-million-dollars a year.
WIK SUMMIT UNDERWAY IN CAIRNS
The Wik summit gets underway in Cairns today with Aboriginal leaders saying that while negotiation is the answer extinguishment of native title is out of the question.

The summit will be opened by the Wik people and will hear the native title concerns of Aboriginal, mining and pastoral groups. ATSIC commission Geoff Clark says Aboriginal expectations are not as high as they once were in terms of ambit claims and they are keen to find common ground.
WIK MEETING JUST THE START
Today's meeting between the Prime Minister and State and Territory leaders is unlikely to agree on a plan of action to deal with the High Court decision on the Wik native title case.
It's the first in a series of meetings John Howard will hold on the ruling which found native title could co-exist with pastoral leases.
Most state leaders want Commonwealth legislation enacted to give some certainty to pastoralists about their leases.
But with meetings with pastoralists, miners and Aboriginal leaders yet to be held, Mr Howard is unlikly to commit to a united Commonwealth strategy.
PRICE RISE FOR IRON ORE GOOD NEWS
Iron-ore producers have managed to negotiate slight price rises for iron-ore fines sold to Japanese steel mills.
Yesterday, BHP and the CRA subsidiary, Hamersley Iron, secured a one percent increase in the price for fines, with a slightly bigger increase for the third major exporter, North.
Export volumes remain unchanged, as do prices for lump iron. BHP says the settlement was satisfactory, given Japan's flat economy, and uncertain prospects for the steel industry.
Some analysts say the price is disappointing, but most regard it as better than expected.
The result comes after disappointment last year, when BHP and other producers took a price cut on another key export commodity, coal.
BELL EXTRADITION PROCESS SLOW, BUT STEADY
Police in South Africa say there's been no bungle in moves to extradite alleged paedophile, Phillip Bell.
Mr Bell will remain in custody in South Africa until early next month, pending the arrival of a formal extradition request, which is still being processed in Australia.
Mr Bell says he'll return to Australia to face 215 outstanding warrants alleging child sex abuse.
Interpol's Inspector Charles Massyn says extradition is a complicated process which takes time.
Inspector Massyn says the extradition papers are in the appropriate channels, and are being processed.
QANTAS PASSENGERS HEAD FOR THE TERRITORY
Qantas has reported a strong increase in demand for flights to a number of its domestic destinations over the past year.
Qantas Holidays General Manager, Ken Rosebery, says passenger numbers heading for the Northern Territory rose by 13 percent, which was the biggest rise.
Queensland's Sunshine Coast recorded an 11 per cent increase, while passenger numbers to Cairns in far north Queensland rose by 10 percent.
The increase for the Gold Coast was five percent, and Mr Rosebery says healthy growth was also noted in the Whitsundays, South Australia and Canberra.
He says there's also been increased demand for short weekend escapes.
